title: Area XI review: Night Operations
intro: These questions walk through a whole night flight: planning, preflight, taxi, cruise, illusions and landing. Some tie in rules the night lesson teaches, like currency, required equipment and VFR minimums.

questions.q: At 6 p.m. your destination reports sky clear, wind calm, temperature 12°C and dew point 10°C. You plan to land there around 10 p.m. What should worry you most?
options: Strong, gusty surface winds after dark
Thunderstorms, because a small spread means unstable air
Fog forming as the ground cools on a clear, calm night
Nothing, because clear skies at 6 p.m. mean good weather all night
questions.why: For a night flight, pay close attention to the temperature/dew point spread. A narrow spread may mean fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]. On clear nights with little or no wind, radiation fog may form as the ground cools and the air reaches its dew point [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]].

questions.q: You made 3 night full-stop landings 60 days ago, so you are night current. Tonight's forecast: 5 miles in haze, strong winds aloft and moderate turbulence. What does FAA guidance say?
options: Currency is only a minimum. Night VFR is best flown only in unrestricted visibility, good winds and no turbulence
Since you are current, the forecast does not matter for a VFR flight
Haze is only a problem in the daytime, because the sun reflects off it
You are legal and safe as long as you carry 45 minutes of reserve fuel
questions.why: The 61.57 rules are minimums. Night flying is a small part of most pilots' time, and marginal weather at night is a big deal, so judge your own need for more practice [[15:20|AC 61-98E para 3.1.2]]. Even for experienced pilots, night VFR should be flown only in unrestricted visibility, favorable winds on the surface and aloft, and no turbulence [[24:231|AFH 11-14]].

questions.q: Sunset is 5:00 p.m. and evening civil twilight ends at 5:28 p.m. Flying solo, you fly three circuits, each with a takeoff and a full-stop landing: 5:10 to 5:20, 5:35 to 5:45, and 6:10 to 6:20 p.m. Which circuits count toward night currency for carrying passengers?
options: All three, because they were all after sunset
The second and third, because they were after civil twilight ended
None, because currency landings must be flown with an instructor aboard
Only the third, because it was more than 1 hour after sunset
questions.why: Passenger currency needs 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings made between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, here after 6:00 p.m. [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. The end of civil twilight (5:28 p.m.) is when 'night' starts for logging, not for this rule [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. You must be the sole manipulator of the controls; no instructor is needed.

questions.q: You are choosing checkpoints for a night cross-country over farm country. Which set does the AFH call excellent night checkpoints?
options: A small unlit pond, a dirt road crossing and a fence line
Airport beacons, lighted towers, town lights and a busy highway
Ridge lines and river bends, since they stand out against dark ground
None. At night you should use only GPS waypoints
questions.why: Rotating beacons at airports, lighted obstructions, lights of cities or towns, and lights from major highway traffic all make excellent night checkpoints [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Unlit features are hard to see in the dark. GPS is useful, but you still check your position, time and fuel as in the day [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

questions.q: Your night route runs along the edge of your sectional chart. Why does the AFH say to also carry the next (adjacent) chart?
options: Town lights can be seen from surprisingly far away, and without the adjacent chart you may not know what they are
Only the adjacent chart shows the pilot-controlled lighting frequency
A regulation requires two charts for every night flight
The adjacent chart lists the night VFR weather minimums
questions.why: The lights of cities and towns can be seen at surprising distances at night. If you can't identify them on the adjacent chart, confusion can result [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. The PCL frequency is in the Chart Supplement, not on sectionals [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

questions.q: Your airplane's landing light is broken. You plan a night flight with friends, not for hire. The airplane has no MEL, and its equipment lists do not require the light. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what makes the flight legal?
options: Nothing extra. Just leave the switch off
Remove or deactivate the light, placard it INOPERATIVE, and have a pilot or mechanic decide it is not a hazard
Nothing will. No light may be broken on a night flight
A special flight permit is needed for every flight until it is fixed
questions.why: A landing light is required at night only if the airplane is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]]. Without an MEL, a broken item that is not required may be deferred if it is removed or deactivated, placarded 'Inoperative,' and a certificated pilot or mechanic determines it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

questions.q: On your night preflight you find the spare-fuse holder empty. Your airplane uses fuses. What does 14 CFR 91.205(c) require before a night VFR flight?
options: Nothing. Spare fuses are needed only when flying for hire
One spare fuse of any kind, kept in the baggage area
One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, that you can reach in flight
Spare fuses are needed only if you plan to use the landing light
questions.why: Night VFR requires one spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, accessible to the pilot in flight [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(6)]]. That applies to every night VFR flight, not just flights for hire.

questions.q: Taxiing at night between blue edge lights, you see a pair of flashing yellow lights, one on each side of the taxiway just ahead. What are they telling you?
options: You have reached the end of the usable taxiway
The taxiway ahead is closed
You are leaving the runway environment
You are coming to a runway holding position
questions.why: Runway guard lights are a pair of elevated flashing yellow lights (or a row of in-pavement yellow lights) at the runway holding position marking [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10]]. They warn you that a runway is just ahead. Blue lights mark taxiway edges [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10]].

questions.q: Taxiing at night at a large, unfamiliar towered airport, the signs no longer match what you expected from the taxi diagram. You are on a taxiway, not a runway. What should you do?
options: Keep rolling slowly while you look down to set up the GPS
Stop, tell ATC, and ask for progressive taxi instructions if needed
Follow the lights of the airplane ahead of you
Speed up so you clear the taxiway before other traffic arrives
questions.why: If you are uncertain of your location, stop (not on a runway), advise ATC and, if needed, ask for progressive taxi. Do heads-down tasks only while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B]]. The AFH adds: if any doubt exists, do not continue the taxi or takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

questions.q: At night the tower tells you, 'Line up and wait.' You turn on all exterior lights except the landing lights. What else does AC 91-73B suggest so a pilot landing behind you can pick you out?
options: Line up about 3 feet left or right of the centerline
Flash your landing lights on and off every few seconds
Stop at the runway edge lights instead of the centerline
Turn off your position lights so you don't blend in with the runway lights
questions.why: At night in line up and wait, consider lining up about 3 feet to the left or right of the centerline so a landing aircraft can tell your airplane apart from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B]]. Turn the landing lights on when cleared for takeoff [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

questions.q: Right after a night takeoff you climb into light haze, and your landing light makes a bright glare in front of the windshield. What does the AFH advise?
options: Leave it on until you reach cruise altitude
Turn off the position lights instead
Make an early turn toward clearer air as soon as you lift off
Turn it off once the climb is well established, unless you need it to be seen by traffic
questions.why: The landing light can reflect off haze, smoke or clouds and distort your view, so turn it off after the climb is well established, unless you are using it for collision avoidance [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Don't turn until you reach a safe maneuvering altitude [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

questions.q: During a night cruise, a passenger shines a bright phone flashlight at the panel for about 2 seconds. Your white strobes have been flashing all flight. Which one hurts your dark adaptation?
options: Only the strobes, because they flash over and over
Only the phone light, because bright light for 1 second or more impairs night vision
Both, equally
Neither, because adaptation can't be lost once it is complete
questions.why: Anticollision flashes last less than 1 second, so they do not impair dark adaptation. A bright light for 1 second or more does impair it for a while. Closing one eye when bright light starts saves that eye's adaptation [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].

questions.q: In cruise on a dark night, you stare at a single light ahead. After about 10 seconds it seems to drift, and you notice you are banking to follow it. What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: Reversible perspective. The light is moving away, so let it go
False horizon. Level your wings on the light
Autokinesis. Keep scanning and don't stare at one light
Flicker vertigo. Turn off your strobes
questions.why: Autokinesis: a still light stared at in the dark seems to move. Movement starts in about 8 to 10 seconds. Visual scanning is the most important fix, and a light should not be stared at for more than 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]. Chasing the false movement can lead to loss of control [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

questions.q: Look at the figure. Over dark country at night, a long level row of ground lights looks like the horizon, and you feel your wings are level with it. What should you do?
options: Trust the attitude indicator, because lights can make a false horizon
Keep the wings level with the row of lights
Descend until the lights look level with the nose
Pick one bright star and fly toward it
questions.why: Ground lights and stars can blend and make a false horizon, so the real horizon may not be where it looks [[24:221|AFH 11-4]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. Rely on the flight instruments, not on what you feel or see outside [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

questions.q: Flying at night near a hazy cloud layer, the flashes of your white strobe lights reflect back into the cockpit and distract you. What may you do?
options: Nothing. Strobes must stay on at all times
Turn off the position lights so the strobes look dimmer
Land at the nearest airport, because the flight is now illegal
Turn the strobes off, because the PIC may do so in the interest of safety
questions.why: Anticollision lights must be on when installed, but they need not be lit when the PIC decides it is safer to turn them off [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]]. The AIM gives adverse reflection from clouds in flight as an example [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. Position lights must stay on from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]].

questions.q: You click the mike 7 times and the pilot-controlled runway lights come on at full brightness. On final they seem too bright. What can you do?
options: Nothing. Pilot-controlled lights can't be adjusted
Click once to turn them off and land with the landing light only
Click 5 times within 5 seconds for medium, or 3 times for the lowest setting
Click 7 times again to step them down
questions.why: Start with 7 clicks for the highest intensity. Then, where the system allows, lower it by keying 5 times (medium or lower) or 3 times (lowest) within 5 seconds [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]]. The lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation and can't be turned off early [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

questions.q: Arriving at an unfamiliar airport at night, you line up on a long, straight row of lights. Then you notice some of the lights are moving. What is the most likely problem?
options: Autokinesis is making the runway lights seem to move
You lined up on a road or a train, a ground lighting illusion
The runway lights are flashing to show the runway is closed
The airport has activated its approach lights for you
questions.why: Lights along a straight path, such as a road or the lights of a moving train, can be mistaken for runway and approach lights [[24:222|AFH 11-5]] [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]. Review the airport layout before the approach, and fly toward the beacon until you can identify the runway lights [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

questions.q: The Chart Supplement shows that your destination's runway slopes up toward the far end. On a night approach, which error should you expect and guard against?
options: Feeling too high, so you fly a lower-than-normal approach
Feeling too low, so you fly a higher-than-normal approach
Thinking the runway is wider than it is
Rounding out late because the runway looks farther away
questions.why: An upsloping runway or terrain makes you feel higher than you are, so you tend to fly a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]]. Expect illusions at unfamiliar airports at night, check the altimeter often, and use a VASI or PAPI if there is one [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

questions.q: You arrive at night at a non-towered airport in Class G airspace. Visibility is 2 statute miles. You will stay in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway, below 1,200 feet AGL. What does 14 CFR 91.155 allow?
options: Nothing. Night VFR in Class G always needs 3 miles
The pattern only if you stay 500 feet below the clouds
The pattern only after you get a special VFR clearance
You may fly the pattern clear of clouds
questions.why: At night in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL the normal minimum is 3 miles and 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. But an airplane may operate clear of clouds with at least 1 mile visibility in a traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].

questions.q: You land long at night on an instrument runway. During the rollout, the white runway edge lights change to yellow. What does that mean?
options: You have left the runway and are on a taxiway
The runway ahead is closed
You are in the caution zone: the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less
You are passing the touchdown zone
questions.why: Runway edge lights are white, but on instrument runways yellow replaces white on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway length, whichever is less, to form a caution zone [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]. Taxiway edge lights are blue [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10]].
